newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's CeBIT sheds light on wired world.
newsitem.headline: Germany's CeBIT sheds light on wired world.

text.p: Around 650,000 visitors should descend on Hanover this week for CeBIT, the world's biggest technology trade fair, but many of the gadgets and services on display make clear that the brave new multimedia world is still more virtual than real
CeBIT, and high-tech trade fairs of its kind, will serve more as a guiding light to a future that seems perpetually around the corner but remains out of reach.

The basic technology needed to really let surfers hang ten in cyberspace already exists, but analysts say it will still be several years before high-speed networks are in place and prices for multimedia services are affordable.

While CeBIT will demonstrate advances in broadband technologies, so-called ATM networks, that are needed to provide true multimedia services to a wide public, the dawn of the multimedia age is still a few years off.

"ATM infrastructure is likely to form the basis on which multiservices broadband, including Internet services, will be delivered to the market," said Margaret Hopkins, of telecoms consultants Analysys in a report to be published in April.

But Hopkins says that ATM - a kind of traffic cop on the Infobahn directing and routing bits of video, graphics, voice and basic data - will be limited to big businesses until around 2000 and not available for most private consumers until 2005.
Until then speed-hungry cybernauts must make do with "narrow-band" networks - using high-speed modems over basic phone lines or Integrated Services Digital Networks (ISDN).

Three times the size of the Fall Comdex show hosted in Las Vegas each year, CeBIT has grown from a tiny office equipment fair in 1970 into a technology Mecca that reflects the explosion of the computing and communications industries.
Among the more than 6,500 exhibitors, the largest single country represented is the United States with over 400 exhibitors. Europeans are worried they are falling behind.

Western Europe's information and communications technologies market (ITC) is expected to grow 7.1 percent in 1997, continuing an upturn that began in 1993, but still a flat growth rate compared to 1996, when the sector grew 7.2 percent.
"Europe really risks losing ground," said Bruno Lamborghini, chairman of the European Information Technology Observatory (EITO), which published the forecast last week.
Hoping to transport the masses of CeBIT visitors and an army of some 9,000 laptop-toting reporters, the German railway has added 120 special trains with around 80,000 seats.
CeBIT organisers have posted information about the event on their World Wide Web site at http://www.cebit.de and it is even possible to search the CeBIT catalogue online.
Despite the gap between the promise of technology and the frustrating reality, CeBIT visitors will be impressed.
Access to the Internet is improving with ISDN and new modem technology that stretches the limits of normal phone lines.
U.S. Robotics will demonstrate its new modem that boosts connections to 56,000 kbs, nearly the speed of digital ISDN.

One of the most important changes in computer technology - compact disc data storage drives using digital video disc technology - are about to replace the standard CD-ROM drive in PCs and will one day retire outdated video recorders.

So-called DVD-ROM drives can hold up to 4.7 gigabytes of data - the size of seven CD-ROMs - extending the potential for multimedia programmes on CD and a later development will allow users to record movies on them in pristine digital quality.
Hitachi will demonstrate what it says is the first DVD-ROM drive for a PC, a sign of what is to come in a few years.
There will also be a special presentation called the "World of Media", which will demonstrate online publishing, multimedia and digital photopraphy.

Telecoms make up the biggest offering at the fair, filling the six largest of the 23 exhibition halls, and this year will focus on ATM, the Internet and host a beauty contest of new firms gearing up for deregulation in the sector next year.
CeBIT organizers have set up an Internet phone for the public -- http://call.cebit.de -- to call anyone in Hanover from anywhere in the world at local rates over the Internet.
The first dual-band mobile phones that allow users to switch between different networks without changing phones will be displayed by Nokia, Ericsson and Motorola.
Computer makers will display a new generation of PC companions -- palm-size computers with the power of desktop computers and the ability to surf the Internet.
